title_zh: 我想你留下，去不去是你的
title_en: I Want You to Stay. The Choice Is Yours.
deck_zh: 他没有装作无所谓，也没有把自己的舍不得变成她的义务。爱里有两份不能混成一份的东西：偏偏是这个人，而这个人仍有她自己的路。
deck_en: He does not pretend to be indifferent. He does not turn his wish into her duty. Loving this particular person and recognizing her life as her own have to remain together.
body_zh: 她在乐团里拉大提琴，他在中学教物理。两个人在一起四年。这年春天，另一座城市的乐团请她去。去了，就是两地；不去，这样的机会也许不会再有。她想了一个星期。有天晚上，她问他：你想我去吗？
他说：我想你留下，这是我的。去不去，是你的。
这句话不轻。他不是终于练成了无所谓，也不是先把难过处理干净，才取得说话的资格。她走前，他有几个晚上睡不着；听她提到以后同台的同事，心里还冒出过一句：你只能是我的。没有说出口，过了一会儿，他自己觉得不对。
这一篇就从这里读爱。他想留下的，不是一个同样温柔、同样会拉琴的人；偏偏是她。可她不是为了替他完成这份爱，才有自己的生活。两样要同时在，不能拿一样替掉另一样。
## 爱这一个人，也让她是她自己
承认一个人有自己的生活，并不就是爱情。老师也可以这样对待学生，我们也可以这样对待街上的陌生人。爱情里还多着那一份：这个人，对我不可替换。换一个同样好的人，不是同一回事。
反过来，不可替换也没有自动包含了另一份。有的人非她不可，便觉得她此后怎么走，都该纳入自己的打算。“我想你留下”可以变成一句实话，也可以紧接着一句“所以你不能去”。正是在这个接续处，两种爱法分开。
物理老师没有把自己的那一半撤掉。他想她留下，照实说了；她想去，也不必先把他的舍不得说成不合理，才能继续想。她的回答会使他重新考虑，会使他难过，可不是她先认可他爱得对，这份爱才算成立。
这也不等于他不想她爱自己。他当然想。想得到回应，和把回应当成自己这样待她的先决条件，不是一件事。不用时时追问“我做得够不够，她有没有还我一样多”，眼睛才可能真的从自己身上移开，去听她这一星期究竟在想什么。
她为什么那么想去，他仍说不全。她提过那里的首席、曲目，也说过想在三十五岁以前试一试。他听见这些，可以问，可以越来越接近，却不能据此宣布：我比你自己更懂你要什么。亲近带来更多材料，不是读穿另一个人的许可证。
这与弗洛姆谈尊重时的一个意思相照：不是让所爱的人朝着服侍我的方向生长，而是让他照自己的方式展开。相照不等于一套现成的爱的教程；这里关心的是，那一次说话有没有把属于她的判断留在她那里。
## 只爱你，不等于有权要求你也只爱我
本系列对这种爱作了一项明确的选择：在这样爱着的那些片刻，所爱的一直是这一个人，而不是在两个人之间轮流。这不是从“没有把人当工具”就能直接推出来的定理，也不是给别人的感情发合格证。它是在说明，这里所读的这一种爱，选择站在什么地方。
持续，也不等于每一秒都在想着她。他上课、改卷子、赶车的时候，不必每一刻都重做一次爱的确认。一次中断不是摇摆。那句没说出口的“你只能是我的”，则显出另一种可能：他也会把自己的方向变成她的尺子。那一刻要另读，不能因此把他整个人或四年的爱一口判完。
若爱的片刻确实在两个人之间轮流，也不能只因曾经说过要一直爱一个，就把这份摇摆抹掉。说清楚正在发生什么，比急着维护一个名目更重要。这种能把对方留给对方的爱并不容易，不是一旦到达，就从此不再失手的等级。
他只爱她，这是他这一端的事。她是否也只爱他，不能由他这份爱直接换来。两个人可以说定彼此排他，那是一份承诺，有它真实的约束与后果；不能拿“不许要求对方的爱”，替已经作出的答应开脱。可仅凭“我只爱你”，仍不能替她签下同一份答应。
如果两个人各自选择只爱对方，两份单向的选择便碰到了。也还不能只看这一点，就判他们彼此真正留出了空间。互相排他可以有不同的来处：愿意，也可能是交换、怕失去，或把与别人的来往都切断。外面看起来一样，不等于里面只有一个答案。
还有一份不该跟着排他的，是对人的承认。物理老师爱她，也仍然承认学生、同事、陌生人有他们自己的路。爱只向着这一个，并不是除她之外的人都成了可用的东西。克尔凯郭尔对情爱偏爱的追问，在这里很有分量；这一篇的回答，是把爱着谁与承认谁分开，不让前者吞掉后者。
## 不等你，也不任你伤害
另有一位做翻译的女子，爱着常有来往的编辑。编辑不爱她，说得很清楚。她的爱不必等他答应才算发生，他的拒绝也没有让他变成一个不值得被当作人的人。可她爱他，并没有给他添一份相同地爱回来的义务。
有一阵，编辑知道她的心意，常在深夜发来急稿，说一句“你最好了”，第二天一早就要。她不因为还爱着，就得把每个夜晚交出去。她可以不接那份稿，不回那个时段的消息，或者不再来往。这些都能与承认他仍有自己的生活同时成立。
所以，单向可以完整，不是说单恋比相爱高，也不是说回应无关紧要，更不是说一个人只要爱得够好，就应当受得住一切。“你若爱我，就什么都该接”，已经在借爱接管她的时间和判断。爱不能变成撤走她边界的理由。
大提琴手那边也一样。物理老师若说“我是为你好，那个乐团不适合你；你还考虑，就是不认我的爱”，他就不只是在提供意见了。他把接受自己的判断，设成了她承认不承认这份爱的证明。她若想另想一想，先得背上不懂爱的罪名。
这与“我担心你去了会后悔”不同。后一句可以把他的理由交给她，仍容许她说：我知道风险，我还是想试。不能仅凭语气温柔或用了“为你好”，就替一句话作好坏判决；也不能只因她后来走了，就说先前的压力没有发生。
另一种冒充，看起来甚至更体贴：他说“你怎样都好，我都行”，其实心里很想她留下，只为保住和气，把自己的判断撤出了商量。这不是给她空间，而是他那一份没有给出来。但偶尔没有开口，并不就叫迁就；何时说、何时暂不说，也可以是自己的判断。
波伏瓦写恋爱中的自我让渡时，让这种失去自己变得很具体。它也不只是某个人不够坚定：社会处境会让牺牲自己成为被赞许、也比较走得通的路。这里不把那些条件抹掉，只辨认眼前的来往里，哪一份声音正在被交出去。多年没有争吵，不能独自证明两个人都仍说得出“不”。
后来，她去了另一座城市。第二年，写来长信，说爱上了另一个人，想结束这段来往。信把退出说得清楚，没有拿过去的答应作一笔已经两清的账。他读完，回了一封短信，没有替她说“这四年你什么也没损失”，也没有把自己的难过拿来定她的去留。
这份爱可以结束。持续不是永久；承认一个人有自己的路，也不要求两个人一直沿同一条路走。她的退出结束了共同的来往，他自己的爱是否结束，仍要从他这一端看。过了几年，他又爱上别人：若前一份确已结束，这是先后；不能反过来，只因有了新爱，就宣布旧爱早已结束。
放开一次接触，不是撤销对方作为人的地位；还爱着，也不使堵住她的去路、找她的同事施压，变成理所当然。有些作用仍会留下：四年的依靠、说过的答应、被听见的愿望。它们需要面对，却不是一张把人叫回来的通行证。
那句话的难处，到这里还在：我想你留下。不是假的，也不必被消灭。去不去，是你的。也不是一句假装大方的话。两半都在，才不是用爱把她收进来，或者为了爱把自己交出去。
body_en: She plays cello in an orchestra. He teaches physics at a secondary school. They have been together for four years when an orchestra in another city invites her to join. Going would mean living apart. Declining might mean losing a chance that will not return. She thinks about it for a week, then asks him one evening: do you want me to go?
“I want you to stay,” he says. “That is mine. Whether you go is yours.”

The sentence is not effortless. He has not become indifferent, or finished being unhappy before allowing himself to speak. There are sleepless nights. Hearing about a musician she will perform with, he briefly thinks, You can only be mine. He does not say it; after a while he recognizes something wrong with the thought.

This essay begins with the two things he is trying to keep together. He does not want a replacement who is equally kind and equally accomplished. He wants her. Yet her life does not exist to complete his love. Neither truth can be substituted for the other.
## This person, with a life of her own

Recognizing someone’s life as their own is not, by itself, romantic love. A teacher can recognize a student in that way; a stranger can recognize another stranger. Love includes something further: this particular person is not interchangeable for me. Someone equally admirable would not amount to the same answer.

The reverse inference fails too. Finding someone irreplaceable does not automatically leave them free. ‘I want you to stay’ can be an honest disclosure. Follow it with ‘Therefore you cannot go,’ and my direction has become a measure imposed on hers.

The physics teacher has not erased his side. He says what he wants. She need not declare his sadness irrational before considering the move. Her answer can matter deeply, unsettle him, make him think again. It is not the certificate he must obtain before his love is allowed to count.

He wants her to love him. Wanting a response is different from making her response a condition of treating her this way. The less he has to keep checking whether he has given enough and received an equal return, the more attention he can spare for what she has actually been thinking about this week.

He still cannot fully explain why she wants the orchestra. She mentions its principal player, its repertoire, a wish to try before turning thirty-five. He can listen, ask, approach her reasons more closely. Closeness does not authorize him to announce that he knows her desire better than she does. More material is not complete access to another person.

There is a useful point of contact with Erich Fromm’s account of respect: wanting the beloved to develop in their own way, rather than into someone who serves us. The present inquiry is not a ready-made lesson in how to love. It asks whether this particular exchange leaves her part in judging with her.
## Loving only you is not a claim to your exclusivity

This series makes an explicit choice about the kind of love being read here: across the moments in which it operates in this way, the beloved remains this person, rather than alternating between two people. That is a philosophical stance, not a theorem deduced simply from refusing to treat people as tools, and not an observer’s license to certify other people’s feelings.

Continuity does not require thinking about her every second. Teaching, marking papers, catching a bus need not repeat a declaration of love. An interruption is not vacillation. The unspoken thought, You can only be mine, points to another possibility: he too can turn his wish into her rule. That moment must be read without pronouncing a final verdict on him or on four years together.

If loving moments really alternate between two people, a declaration of constancy cannot erase the wavering. Nor is this way of loving a permanent rank achieved once and retained forever. Making room for another person is difficult. Failure remains possible.

His loving only her cannot, on its own, purchase her loving only him. They can promise exclusivity, and such a promise has genuine force and consequences; this distinction does not excuse ignoring an agreement. But ‘I love only you’ cannot supply a matching promise in her name.

Where each freely chooses the other, two independently held choices meet. Their exclusivity alone still cannot certify the encounter described here. Exclusivity can have other sources: exchange, fear of loss, isolation from everyone else. An identical appearance does not settle what holds it up.

One thing must not become exclusive: recognition of people as having lives of their own. He loves her, but his students, colleagues and strangers do not consequently become usable objects. Kierkegaard’s challenge to preferential love presses precisely here. This essay responds by distinguishing the person loved from the people recognized, rather than allowing love for one to swallow recognition of the rest.
## Not waiting for you does not mean enduring everything

Consider someone else: a translator who loves an editor she regularly works with. He has clearly said he does not love her. Her love need not wait for his approval before it has happened. His refusal does not reduce his standing as a person. Her love does not give him a matching obligation to love her back.

Knowing how she feels, he begins sending urgent work late at night: ‘You’re the best,’ followed by a deadline the next morning. Loving him does not require surrendering every evening. She can decline the manuscript, stop answering at that hour, or end contact. None requires her to revoke his standing as someone whose life is his own.

A one-way love can be complete without being superior to mutual love. Completeness does not mean that a response is unimportant, or that enough love should enable someone to bear unlimited demands. ‘If you loved me, you would accept anything’ recruits love to occupy her time and judgment. It cannot be a reason to remove her boundaries.

Return to the cellist. Suppose her partner says, ‘That orchestra is wrong for you. I love you, so you cannot go. Even considering it means you reject my love.’ Accepting his judgment has now become the test of acknowledging his love. She must first face a charge of not understanding him before she can think differently.

‘I am worried you might regret it’ can do something else: offer a reason she may consider and decline. A gentle voice does not settle the difference. Neither does her eventual departure make an earlier pressure disappear. We need to read what the words did at the time, not award them a verdict from tone or outcome.

Another imitation looks especially considerate. He says, ‘Whatever you want is fine,’ while withdrawing what he actually thinks merely to preserve harmony. That is not the same as leaving her room; his own contribution has disappeared. Silence on one occasion proves nothing, however. Choosing when to speak can also be his own judgment.

Beauvoir’s account of surrendering oneself in love makes the danger vivid. It cannot all be reduced to an individual’s failure of firmness: social circumstances can reward self-sacrifice and make it the available path. Keeping those conditions visible, we can still ask whose voice is being handed over here. Years without arguments do not prove that both people can still say no.

She takes the job. In the second year away, she sends a long letter: she has fallen in love with someone else and wants to end their relationship. The departure is made clear; the earlier promises and reliance are not simply declared settled. He answers without announcing that she has lost nothing over four years, or using his grief to decide her next step.

This love can end. Continuity is not permanence. Her departure ends their ongoing shared involvement; whether his love ends is a further question at his end. Years later he loves someone else. If the earlier love has ended, this is succession, not vacillation. A new love cannot retrospectively prove that the former one had already ended.

Ending contact need not cancel recognition. Continuing to love does not entitle him to obstruct her departure or pressure her through colleagues. What remains—the reliance, the promises, the wishes once heard—needs to be faced. It is not a pass authorizing him to bring her back.

Both halves of the sentence remain difficult. I want you to stay: real, and not something that must be extinguished. The choice is yours: not a performance of generosity. Keeping both is different from gathering her into my love, or handing myself over in its name.
